abstract: How semigamy generates haploids during double fertilization has remained elusive for more than six decades. Here, we identify Gamete Expressed 1 (GEX1) as the gene underlying semigamy and show that it mediates dual-origin haploid induction in cotton. A naturally occurring mutation in GEX1 disrupts normal nuclear membrane fusion during fertilization, resulting in delayed or incomplete karyogamy. Cytological analyses reveal that delayed karyogamy allows the closely apposed but unfused gametic nuclei to undergo independent mitotic divisions, giving rise to maternal haploids, paternal haploids, and chimeric progeny. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated disruption of GEX1 reproduced the characteristic defects in nuclear fusion and enabled both maternal and paternal haploid induction within a single generation. Together, our findings uncover a genetically tractable mechanism underlying semigamy that links nuclear membrane fusion dynamics to haploid formation and establish a versatile strategy for rapidly generating doubled haploids from both parental genomes to accelerate crop breeding.
